To make this roadmap immediately actionable, we need to bridge the gap between the defined tooling layout and the actual keystrokes required to bootstrap it. The plan is sound, but pacing the implementation is key to avoiding a massive, un-reviewable tooling dump.

Here is how to translate the retrospective into a concrete execution plan:

1. Bootstrap the TDD Boundary

Applying an Evolutionary Modular Dimensional TDD framework to this phase ensures that the contracts dictate the implementation, rather than building generators in the dark. Instead of writing the extraction scripts first, start by defining the rigid boundaries:

  • Draft the Schema: Create the raw schemas/diagnostic-report-v1alpha1.schema.json file manually. This acts as your source of truth.
  • Write the Failing Tests: Use node:test to build a small suite that attempts to validate known valid and invalid Rust outputs (the fixtures) against this new schema.
  • Build the Tool: Only once the tests are failing should you write demo/tools/generate-contract-data.mjs to satisfy the schema constraints and make the tests pass.

2. Terminal Environment Integration

The proposed demo/tools/ directory is clean, but manually typing out node demo/tools/generate-contract-data.mjs --check repeatedly introduces friction. Wiring these directly into your Fish shell terminal environment will keep the feedback loop instantaneous.

You can set up custom functions or abbreviations for the heavy-rotation scripts to keep the ergonomics high while maintaining a dependency-free repository:

  • abbr -a tgen 'node demo/tools/generate-contract-data.mjs'
  • abbr -a tchk 'node demo/tools/generate-contract-data.mjs --check'
  • abbr -a tserve 'node demo/tools/serve-preview.mjs'

3. Establish the Unified Gatekeeper

The retrospective correctly mandates that all generation tools must have a non-writing --check mode. To make this actionable for future CI or local verification, wrap them immediately in a single executable gatekeeper (e.g., demo/tools/verify-all.mjs or a simple shell script).

  • It should sequentially run node --check on the core modules, execute the node:test suites, and trigger the --check flags on your generators.
  • If any step fails, it exits with a non-zero code. This guarantees that drift, syntax errors, and contract mismatches are caught in one command before a commit is finalized.

4. Define the Minimal Viable Corpus

For the fuzzer and corpus generator (Tool #7), don't try to account for every edge case on day one. Start with a "Minimal Viable Corpus" array directly in the testing file:

  1. One perfect "happy path" report.
  2. One report missing a required check.
  3. One report with a null metadata field. Once the schema validator can handle these three consistently, you can expand into the more complex mutations like extreme timestamps and duplicated IDs.
